transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, my wife is the one who wanted me to come talk to you. It’s mostly about the men down at the domino table. I’ve been playing with those boys for... oh, must be twenty years now, ever since I stopped working. Charlie, he always tries to hide the double six, but I catch him. His hands are all curled up with arthritis, poor fella, so he fumbles the tiles a lot. 

But lately... well, I came because they've been slipping in these little messages when they play, and they're meant just for me. And it's not just them, it's the radio announcer too. I listen to the AM station every morning. You know, they don't make radios like they used to. My daddy had one of those big wooden ones, took up half the parlor, had the glowing tubes in the back... 

But anyway, the fella on the radio, he does it too. He gives me messages. My wife, she gets all huffed up and says it is just regular talk, but I know better. I know they are warning me to be careful. I just... I don't know why they can't just come out and say it plain instead of talking in codes.
Can you tell me more about the messages you receive from the men at the domino table and the radio announcer? Do you believe they are specifically targeting you or trying to harm you in some way?

Well, no, I don't think they want to hurt me. It's more like... like a warning. Charlie will play a tile, maybe a four-blank, and the way he taps it on the table—tap, tap, tap—it means I need to watch my back. And the radio fella, he'll be reading the farm report or the weather, and he'll pause just a second too long before he says 'storm.' It's meant for me. It's a sign to be careful. 

My wife, bless her heart, she just sighs and tells me to turn the dial. She never did like AM radio anyway. Always preferred her gospel records. We used to have a record player, one of those portable ones in a little suitcase. We took it on a picnic down by the lake back in '62. The water was so clear back then, not like now with all the algae and the motorboats making a racket. We had fried chicken... she made the best fried chicken, cooked it in lard, none of this vegetable oil nonsense they push nowadays. 

But, uh, where was I? Oh, the messages. Yes, even when she says it's just regular talk, I know better. They're telling me to be careful, plain as day. I just wish they wouldn't beat around the bush so much.
Do you feel like the messages you're receiving are part of a bigger plan or that someone is trying to influence your thoughts or actions in any way?

Well, a bigger plan... I suppose you could call it that, yes. Like I said, the men at the domino table and the radio announcer, they're giving me these little messages. It's meant for me, to warn me to be careful. My wife tells me it's just talk, but I know it's not. I know it. 

Speaking of plans, though, my wife's been planning to redo the back porch. We've had that same screened-in porch since we bought the place. I put the screens up myself, you know. Bought the mesh down at the old hardware store on Main Street. Old man Henderson ran it back then. He had this big jar of peppermints on the counter, the kind wrapped in clear plastic. You don't see those much anymore. Now everything is in a big box store, no personal touch. Henderson knew exactly what size nails you needed just by looking at the wood you brought in. 

But, uh, yes, the messages. They are definitely trying to tell me something, trying to get me to be careful about... well, whatever it is they're warning me about. I just know it's real, no matter what my wife says.
Do you feel like the messages you're getting are all connected, like they're part of a single plan or scheme that someone has put together specifically for you?

Well, connected... I suppose they must be. I mean, Charlie at the domino table and the fella on the radio, they're both doing it, right? Giving me those little messages meant just for me. Warning me to be careful. My wife, she just shakes her head and says it's regular talk, but I know what I hear. I know they're warning me. 

You know, speaking of being careful, I used to tell my boys that all the time when they were learning to drive. We had this old Ford pickup, a '54, painted the color of a bruised apple. The clutch on that thing was stiffer than a frozen boot. You had to really stomp on it, or it would grind the gears something awful. My oldest, Tommy, he ground 'em so bad once I thought the whole transmission was gonna fall right out onto the dirt road. We used to drive down to the creek to fish for catfish. Used stink bait... boy, did that stuff smell. Get it on your hands and you wouldn't get it off for a week. 

But yes, doctor, the messages. They're connected, sure as I'm sitting here. They're all trying to tell me the same thing, to watch my step. Even if my wife doesn't hear it, I know they're warning me.
Do you think the messages you're hearing are being put into your mind by someone or something else, like through the radio or when you're playing dominoes?

Put into my mind? No, no, they don't have to get inside my head to do it. Like I was telling you, doctor, I came in here because the men at the domino table and sometimes the radio announcer give these little messages meant for me. It's right there out in the open. And even when my wife says it is just talk, I know they are warning me to be careful. I just hear it with my own two ears, plain as day. 

My hearing's always been sharp, you know. Never needed one of those hearing aids. Now my brother Frank, he went deaf as a post by the time he was sixty. Worked in a metal stamping plant up north. Big heavy presses coming down all day long—bam, bam, bam. Shook the whole concrete floor. They didn't give 'em earplugs back then, you just stuffed a bit of cotton in there if your head started ringing too bad. Frank ended up having to read lips mostly. He was a crackerjack mechanic, though. Could rebuild a carburetor blindfolded. Used to lay all the little springs and screws out on a clean rag right on the kitchen table. His wife, Mary, she'd get so mad about the smell of gasoline in the house... she'd chase him out to the garage with a broom. They had a nice garage, detached, with a little wood stove in the corner. Kept it real warm in the winter.

Do you feel like the messages you're hearing are being placed into your thoughts by someone or something else, or do you experience them as coming from outside yourself, like through the radio or during conversations?

Well, like I was just saying, they're not putting thoughts in my head. It's coming from outside, right out in the open. The men at the domino table, the fella on the radio... they just give these little messages meant for me. I hear them talking, warning me to be careful. My wife, she keeps telling me it's just regular talk, but I know what I'm hearing. 

Speaking of hearing things, we used to have this old Zenith radio in the living room. Big wooden cabinet, took up half the wall. You had to wait for the tubes to warm up before you could hear anything. We'd sit around it on Sunday evenings and listen to the programs. Jack Benny, The Lone Ranger... those were the days. My mother would be knitting in her chair, always making these scratchy wool sweaters. I hated wearing them, they made my neck itch terribly. She'd use this dark green yarn she got on sale down at the five and dime. The lady who worked there, Mrs. Gable, she had a glass eye. Always stared right through you. She gave me a piece of hard candy once, but it tasted like mothballs. 

But, uh, no, nobody's putting thoughts in my head. I just hear the messages they're sending me to be careful, plain as day.
Do you believe that the messages you're hearing are part of a special mission or that you have been chosen for a specific purpose?

Well, a special mission... I don't know if I'd call it a mission, exactly, but sometimes I get so sure that I'm the only one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. It's like I have this special gift, you know? A gift for making people listen and follow my plans. I just know I can fix things around here if they'd just pay attention. 

We used to have block parties every summer when I was younger. The whole street would come out. Mrs. Higgins would make her famous potato salad. It had too much mustard for my taste, but everyone else seemed to love it. She lived in that blue house on the corner, the one with the big oak tree in the front yard. That tree was struck by lightning back in '78. Split it right down the middle, sounded like a cannon going off. Woke the whole street up. The fire department had to come out because a branch fell on old Mr. Peterson's Buick. Ruined the roof completely. He was so mad he tried to sue the city, but you can't sue God for lightning, can you? That's what the judge told him anyway.

But yeah, I just feel like I've got this... this ability to get people organized, to get them to follow my lead. Like a special gift.
Do you believe that you have any special powers or abilities that other people don't have?

Well, like I was saying, it's not like I can fly or read minds or anything out of a comic book. But I do get sure, I mean really sure, that I am the one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. It's like I have a special gift for making people listen and follow my plans. 

I was actually trying to explain this to the mailman the other day. He's a new fella, young kid, maybe twenty-two. Drives one of those new electric mail trucks. They're so quiet, you don't even hear them coming down the street. Not like the old ones that used to rattle and sputter. My dog, Buster—God rest his soul—used to hear the mail truck from three blocks away and start howling. Buster was a good dog, part beagle, part something else. We found him shivering under a parked car in the grocery store parking lot. The old A&P that used to be down on Main Street. They tore it down in the nineties to build a pharmacy, which is funny because now there's a pharmacy on every corner. You can't throw a rock without hitting a place selling aspirin and greeting cards. 

But anyway, yeah, I just have this gift, you know? A way of getting people to see my plans and follow along.
Do you feel like you have any kind of special connection with a higher power or that you've been chosen by God or any divine figure for a specific purpose?

No, no, nothing like that. I'm not a prophet or anything. I mean, I believe in the good Lord, sure, but He hasn't come down to give me any special orders or tap me on the shoulder. 

We used to go to St. Jude's every Sunday, though. Beautiful old church. They had these big stained glass windows all along the east wall. One of them got broke back in... oh, must have been '89. A bunch of kids playing baseball in the empty lot next door hit a foul ball right through the face of Saint Peter. The priest, Father Thomas, he was furious. He had this little vein in his forehead that would bulge out when he got mad. He drove a Ford Pinto, you know. Pale yellow. Worst car ever made, those Pintos. My brother-in-law Charlie bought one brand new and the heater never worked. Charlie was a pipefitter down at the plant, always had cold hands anyway. He used to carry a big metal thermos of black coffee just to keep his fingers warm on the job. Black coffee, no sugar. Said sugar was for hummingbirds. He had a glass hummingbird feeder on his back porch, used to boil the sugar water himself on the stove... 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, God's not giving me any special divine purpose or talking to me from on high. Just my own gift for getting the neighborhood together, that's all.
Do you believe that you are better or more important than other people, or that you have a role that no one else can fulfill?

Well, I don't know about being more important, like I'm a king or a mayor or something. But I do get this feeling, this absolute certainty, that I'm the only one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. Like I've got this special gift for making folks listen and follow my plans. 

It's sort of like how my Uncle Frank used to get everyone to listen to him. He was a loud man, Frank. Worked on the railroad for forty years, laying track out west. He lost half of his left pinky finger in a coupling accident back in '52. Never stopped him from playing the accordion, though. He'd bring that heavy old thing out at Christmas and play polkas until my aunt would threaten to hide it in the attic. She kept all her old sewing patterns up in that attic. Hundreds of them, mostly from the sixties. She made me a suit once, for my cousin's wedding. It was a terrible shade of brown, like mud, but I wore it anyway because she worked so hard on it. The wedding was down at the VFW hall, the one with the leaky roof over the dance floor... 

But yeah, I just know I'm the one who can get everyone on the same page. It's my special gift.
Do you feel that you have a unique role or importance that others don't, like you're meant to lead or guide people in a way no one else can?

Well, like I keep telling you, Doc, I ain't no president or nothing. But I just got this... this absolute knowing that I'm the one meant to bring the whole neighborhood together. People just naturally listen to me and want to follow the plans I make. 

You gotta have good plans, you know. You can't build a house without a blueprint. My daddy was a carpenter, built half the houses on the south side of town with his own two hands. He used one of those wooden folding rulers, kept it right in his overalls pocket. Those overalls always smelled like pine sawdust and chewing tobacco. Red Man, that was his brand. He'd spit it right into an old Folgers coffee can he kept by the porch steps. Mother hated that can. She used to grow petunias all around the porch, bright pink ones. Said the soil was good there because of the rain runoff from the gutters. We had to clean those gutters out every autumn, wet leaves piled up thick from the big oak tree out front. That tree got struck by lightning back in the summer of '65, split right down the middle like a piece of firewood... 

But, uh, yeah. I just know I'm the one to lead the neighborhood. It's my gift.
Do you feel like others in the neighborhood recognize your ability to lead, or do you think they don’t listen to you as much as they should?

Well, you know, it depends on the week. Some weeks I wake up feeling so bright and important, like I've got the sun right in my chest. I laugh loud, I talk fast, and I'm just ready to get things moving. But if folks don't listen, if they slow me down or start questioning my plans, I get real sharp with them. Real snappy. 

It reminds me of how my old dog Buster used to get. Buster was a beagle mix, had one blue eye and one brown eye. Smartest dog you ever saw, but he had no patience for the neighbor's cat. That cat was a big orange tabby, looked like a pumpkin with legs. It used to sit right on the fence post and just stare at Buster. Used to drive him crazy. Buster would bark until his voice went hoarse. We kept him on a long chain in the yard, attached to this old metal stake my daddy drove into the ground. Daddy used a sledgehammer for that. Heavy thing, probably weighed twenty pounds. He bought it at the hardware store downtown, the one Mr. Henderson used to run before he retired and moved to Florida. Florida's too hot, if you ask me. All that humidity, makes your joints ache. My cousin Martha went to Florida once for a vacation, brought back a whole bag of those little seashell soaps. Looked pretty, but they didn't lather worth a darn... 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, when I'm feeling bright and fast, I just get irritable if people don't keep up with me or question what I'm doing.
Do you often feel that you are more capable, talented, or destined for great things compared to other people your age?

Well, like I've been trying to tell you, Doc, I don't know about "great things" like being on the television or nothing. But compared to other fellas my age? Sure. I just get this absolute certainty that I'm the only one who can bring this whole neighborhood back together. I've got that special gift, you see, to make people listen and follow my plans. 

Most folks my age, they're just sitting around playing bingo down at the church basement. St. Agnes, over on 4th street. They use those little ink dabbers now, you know? Red and purple ink everywhere. Back in the day, we used those little plastic chips, the translucent red ones. You had to be real careful, because if somebody bumped the folding table, your whole card was ruined. Old man Higgins used to bump the table on purpose if he was losing. He had a terrible temper, Higgins did. Worked at the auto plant until they closed it down in '78. Drove a pale blue Ford Falcon. The muffler on that thing was completely shot, sounded like a tractor coming down the avenue. 

My brother had a tractor, a John Deere. Used it to plow his long gravel driveway in the winter. The winter of '78 was a bad one, let me tell you. Snow was piled all the way up to the porch railing. We had to melt snow on the woodstove just to have water to flush the toilet because the pipes froze solid. Took three days for the county plow to make it out to his place... 

But, anyway, I ain't just sitting around waiting to get old like the rest of them. I got my plans for the neighborhood, and I know I'm the one to do it.
Do you often feel that you are better than other people or that you have abilities or importance that others don't?

Well, Doc, I feel like a broken record here, but yeah, it's just like I said. I don't think I'm better than nobody in a high-and-mighty way, but I do get this absolute certainty that I'm the only one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. It's like I have a special gift, you know? A gift for making people listen and follow my plans. 

You need a good plan if you're gonna fix things up. Like when they tried to fix up the old bandstand in the park. They hired this contractor from two towns over, fella named Miller or maybe Milner. Drove a shiny new pickup truck, didn't have a speck of dirt on it. Now, you tell me, how's a man gonna do hard work if his truck is that clean? My daddy's truck was always covered in mud and drywall dust. It was a '54 Chevy, step-side. He painted it forest green himself using a brush, not a spray gun. You could see the brush strokes if you looked real close, especially on the tailgate. 

That tailgate was heavy, too. We used to sit on it and eat watermelon in the summer. The kind with the black seeds, not these seedless ones they have now. Seedless watermelon just don't taste right, if you ask me. It's like they bred all the flavor right out of it. We used to have watermelon seed spitting contests. My brother could spit a seed clear across the driveway, hit the side of the garage. The garage had this old tin roof that would rattle like crazy when the wind blew hard. Sounded like a freight train was coming right through the yard. 

But, uh, anyway... yeah. I just know I got that special gift to lead folks around here. I'm the one who can do it.
Do you feel that your ability to lead or bring people together is something truly extraordinary, something that most people couldn't do and that sets you apart from others?

Well, Doc, I feel like we're going round in circles here, like a dog chasing its own tail. But yes, I suppose you could say it sets me apart. I just get this absolute certainty, like a bell ringing clear in my head, that I'm the one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. Like I've got this special gift for making folks listen and fall in line with my plans. 

It's a lot like how my uncle Charlie used to call the square dances down at the Grange Hall. Charlie had a voice like a foghorn, you could hear him over the fiddle and the stomping boots no problem. He'd wear these bright red suspenders and a bolo tie with a piece of turquoise the size of a robin's egg. He bought that tie out in Arizona when he went to see the Grand Canyon. Said the canyon was just a big hole in the ground, but he sure liked the jewelry. 

Charlie's wife, Aunt Bessie, she used to make the best peach cobbler for those dances. She'd use fresh peaches from the tree in their backyard, not the canned stuff. The canned stuff is always too mushy, tastes like tin. Bessie's cobbler had this thick crust on top, sprinkled with coarse sugar that would crunch when you bit into it. She baked it in this big cast-iron Dutch oven that she inherited from her grandmother. That pot must have weighed thirty pounds empty. You had to use two hands just to lift the lid. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I just have that special gift, you know? That certainty that I'm the one to lead the neighborhood.
Have you noticed any other people or things in your life sending you messages or being part of this warning system, outside of the domino table and the radio?

Well, no, not really anything else. It's just like I was telling you, it's the men at the domino table, and sometimes that announcer on the radio, they're the ones giving me those little messages meant just for me. My wife, she always says it is just talk, but I know they are warning me to be careful. You gotta be careful these days. 

Especially down at the center where we play. We use the double-nine dominoes, you know. A lot of folks only use the double-six, but you need the double-nine if you've got a full table. My granddaddy had a set made of real bone. They came in this heavy wooden box with a little brass latch on the front. That latch was always sticking, though. You had to pry it open with a butter knife just to get the pieces out. We had these old butter knives with the yellow handles... bakelite, I think they called it. You don't see bakelite much anymore. Everything now is just cheap plastic. 

My wife bought a new spatula last week and the darn thing melted right in the skillet while she was frying eggs. She likes her eggs sunny-side up, but the edges have to be real crispy. You gotta use bacon grease for that, none of that vegetable oil nonsense. My regular doctor told me to watch my cholesterol, but I figure at eighty-four, I've earned a little bacon grease. 

But, uh, no... no other things sending messages. Just the radio and the domino fellas. I know they're looking out for me with those warnings, even if my wife thinks it's nothing.
Do you feel that the people sending you these messages are working together with you toward a common goal, like you're all part of something bigger?

Well, Doc, I wouldn't say we're all part of some big grand plan or working together like that. No, it's just like I said before... I came because the men at the domino table, and sometimes that fella on the radio, they just give me these little messages. They're meant just for me, you see. My wife, she always says it's just talk, just old men flapping their gums, but I know they are warning me to be careful. 

You really do have to be careful. Like when you're crossing Elm Street down by the pharmacy. They put in that new crosswalk, but they didn't put a stoplight, just those yellow flashing lights. Nobody stops for yellow flashing lights. It's like a racetrack down there. Young kids in those little imported cars with the loud mufflers. Sounds like a swarm of angry bees coming down the road. I used to have a car that sounded like that, but it was because the exhaust pipe rusted clear through. It was a '68 Ford Fairlane. Bought it off a fella who used to race it out at the dirt track on weekends. 

He painted the whole thing primer gray. Never got around to putting a real coat of paint on it. Said primer was lighter, made the car go faster. I don't know about all that, but it sure was ugly. My wife hated that car. Refused to ride in it to church on Sundays. Said she wouldn't be caught dead arriving at the Lord's house in a primer-gray jalopy. We had to take her sister's car instead. Her sister drove this big old Buick LeSabre, the kind with the bench seats that felt like a living room sofa. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right. No, we ain't working together or nothing. It's just them warning me to be careful with those little messages. I just know what I hear, even if the wife don't believe it.
Do you think the messages you receive have a larger purpose or that they are part of a more organized effort to communicate with you?

Well, no, I wouldn't call it some big organized effort or some grand purpose. It's just like I've been telling you, Doc. I came in because those fellas at the domino table, and sometimes that fella on the radio, they just slip in these little messages meant just for me. My wife, she keeps saying it's just talk, just old men making noise, but I know what I hear. I know they're warning me to be careful. 

You really can't be too careful, especially with the weather turning. When the barometer drops, my left knee starts acting up. It's like a built-in weather station, better than the meteorologist on Channel 4. That fella on Channel 4, he always wears these flashy striped ties. Makes my eyes go funny just looking at him. My grandfather used to wear a tie every single day, even when he was just sitting on the front porch whittling. He’d whittle these little wooden whistles out of hickory branches. 

He had this pocket knife, a Case knife, bone handle. He kept it so sharp you could shave with it. He actually did shave with it once, just to prove he could, on a bet with my uncle. My uncle lost five dollars that day. Five dollars was a lot of money back then. You could buy a whole week's worth of groceries for five dollars. Now you can't even buy a decent cup of coffee for that. They charge you an arm and a leg for a cup of coffee, and half the time it's lukewarm. 

But anyway... what was it you asked? Oh, right. No, it's not a big organized thing. Just those little messages from the domino table and the radio, warning me to be careful, no matter what my wife thinks.
Do you think the messages you're getting from the domino table and the radio happen randomly, or do you believe they follow a pattern or schedule that you've noticed?

Well, I wouldn't say there's a schedule, like a bus timetable or anything. It's just like I keep saying, Doc. I came because the men at the domino table, and sometimes that fella on the radio, they give me these little messages meant just for me. My wife, she always says it's just talk, but I know they are warning me to be careful. 

You gotta be careful, especially about schedules. Reminds me of when I used to take the Greyhound bus down to see my brother in Shreveport. That bus was never on schedule. You'd sit at the station for hours. The station had these hard wooden benches, the kind that make your backside numb after about ten minutes. And they always smelled like floor wax and stale cigarette smoke. Back then, everybody smoked. You could buy a pack of Chesterfields for a quarter out of a vending machine. 

Those vending machines had a heavy metal knob you had to pull, and it made this loud chunking sound. CHUNK. And the pack would drop down. Sometimes a pack of matches would come with it, tucked right under the cellophane. They don't make matches like they used to, either. Now they just bend when you try to strike them. My brother used to collect matchbooks from every place he went. Had a whole fishbowl full of them sitting on his television set. It was one of those big console TVs, the kind in the wooden cabinet that looked like a piece of furniture. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, right, a pattern. No, no real pattern to it. Just those warnings I get from the domino table and the radio, telling me to be careful, even if the wife don't see it.

inference_history.note: The patient reports receiving coded messages from people he plays dominoes with and a radio announcer, which suggests possible delusional or paranoid thinking. This supports the inclusion of Schizophrenia (F20.9) as a provisional diagnosis, as well as Delusional disorder (F22.0), other persistent delusional disorders (F22.8), and unspecified persistent delusional disorder (F22.9). No prior candidates existed for comparison.

The patient continues to describe experiences consistent with delusional ideation, specifically referential thinking (e.g., messages from the radio and domino games) and grandiosity (e.g., belief in a special ability to organize the neighborhood). No new symptoms inconsistent with the previous candidates were identified, and no definitive exclusion of any of the prior diagnoses occurred. The patient does not report clear hallucinations, thought insertion, or other first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia, keeping the differential in the realm of delusional disorder and related entities.

The patient continues to describe experiences of receiving messages from external sources (domino players, radio announcer), which are perceived as warnings. There is no evidence of delusions of grandeur, influence, or thought insertion, which reduces the likelihood of F20.9 (Schizophrenia, unspecified). The patient denies any divine or supernatural involvement, ruling out specific delusional themes that might point more strongly to F22.0 if not already under consideration. The delusional themes remain non-bizarre and persistent, supporting the retention of F22.0, F22.8, and F22.9 as possible candidates.

patient.answer:
Well, no, I don't think they want to hurt me. It's more like... like a warning. Charlie will play a tile, maybe a four-blank, and the way he taps it on the table—tap, tap, tap—it means I need to watch my back. And the radio fella, he'll be reading the farm report or the weather, and he'll pause just a second too long before he says 'storm.' It's meant for me. It's a sign to be careful. 

My wife, bless her heart, she just sighs and tells me to turn the dial. She never did like AM radio anyway. Always preferred her gospel records. We used to have a record player, one of those portable ones in a little suitcase. We took it on a picnic down by the lake back in '62. The water was so clear back then, not like now with all the algae and the motorboats making a racket. We had fried chicken... she made the best fried chicken, cooked it in lard, none of this vegetable oil nonsense they push nowadays. 

But, uh, where was I? Oh, the messages. Yes, even when she says it's just regular talk, I know better. They're telling me to be careful, plain as day. I just wish they wouldn't beat around the bush so much.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for further elaboration on the patient's delusional beliefs about the messages and whether they involve a larger scheme or thought influence, which directly relates to the symptom of delusions.

patient.answer:
Well, a bigger plan... I suppose you could call it that, yes. Like I said, the men at the domino table and the radio announcer, they're giving me these little messages. It's meant for me, to warn me to be careful. My wife tells me it's just talk, but I know it's not. I know it. 

Speaking of plans, though, my wife's been planning to redo the back porch. We've had that same screened-in porch since we bought the place. I put the screens up myself, you know. Bought the mesh down at the old hardware store on Main Street. Old man Henderson ran it back then. He had this big jar of peppermints on the counter, the kind wrapped in clear plastic. You don't see those much anymore. Now everything is in a big box store, no personal touch. Henderson knew exactly what size nails you needed just by looking at the wood you brought in. 

But, uh, yes, the messages. They are definitely trying to tell me something, trying to get me to be careful about... well, whatever it is they're warning me about. I just know it's real, no matter what my wife says.

patient.answer:
Well, connected... I suppose they must be. I mean, Charlie at the domino table and the fella on the radio, they're both doing it, right? Giving me those little messages meant just for me. Warning me to be careful. My wife, she just shakes her head and says it's regular talk, but I know what I hear. I know they're warning me. 

You know, speaking of being careful, I used to tell my boys that all the time when they were learning to drive. We had this old Ford pickup, a '54, painted the color of a bruised apple. The clutch on that thing was stiffer than a frozen boot. You had to really stomp on it, or it would grind the gears something awful. My oldest, Tommy, he ground 'em so bad once I thought the whole transmission was gonna fall right out onto the dirt road. We used to drive down to the creek to fish for catfish. Used stink bait... boy, did that stuff smell. Get it on your hands and you wouldn't get it off for a week. 

But yes, doctor, the messages. They're connected, sure as I'm sitting here. They're all trying to tell me the same thing, to watch my step. Even if my wife doesn't hear it, I know they're warning me.

patient.answer:
Put into my mind? No, no, they don't have to get inside my head to do it. Like I was telling you, doctor, I came in here because the men at the domino table and sometimes the radio announcer give these little messages meant for me. It's right there out in the open. And even when my wife says it is just talk, I know they are warning me to be careful. I just hear it with my own two ears, plain as day. 

My hearing's always been sharp, you know. Never needed one of those hearing aids. Now my brother Frank, he went deaf as a post by the time he was sixty. Worked in a metal stamping plant up north. Big heavy presses coming down all day long—bam, bam, bam. Shook the whole concrete floor. They didn't give 'em earplugs back then, you just stuffed a bit of cotton in there if your head started ringing too bad. Frank ended up having to read lips mostly. He was a crackerjack mechanic, though. Could rebuild a carburetor blindfolded. Used to lay all the little springs and screws out on a clean rag right on the kitchen table. His wife, Mary, she'd get so mad about the smell of gasoline in the house... she'd chase him out to the garage with a broom. They had a nice garage, detached, with a little wood stove in the corner. Kept it real warm in the winter.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just saying, they're not putting thoughts in my head. It's coming from outside, right out in the open. The men at the domino table, the fella on the radio... they just give these little messages meant for me. I hear them talking, warning me to be careful. My wife, she keeps telling me it's just regular talk, but I know what I'm hearing. 

Speaking of hearing things, we used to have this old Zenith radio in the living room. Big wooden cabinet, took up half the wall. You had to wait for the tubes to warm up before you could hear anything. We'd sit around it on Sunday evenings and listen to the programs. Jack Benny, The Lone Ranger... those were the days. My mother would be knitting in her chair, always making these scratchy wool sweaters. I hated wearing them, they made my neck itch terribly. She'd use this dark green yarn she got on sale down at the five and dime. The lady who worked there, Mrs. Gable, she had a glass eye. Always stared right through you. She gave me a piece of hard candy once, but it tasted like mothballs. 

But, uh, no, nobody's putting thoughts in my head. I just hear the messages they're sending me to be careful, plain as day.

patient.answer:
Well, a special mission... I don't know if I'd call it a mission, exactly, but sometimes I get so sure that I'm the only one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. It's like I have this special gift, you know? A gift for making people listen and follow my plans. I just know I can fix things around here if they'd just pay attention. 

We used to have block parties every summer when I was younger. The whole street would come out. Mrs. Higgins would make her famous potato salad. It had too much mustard for my taste, but everyone else seemed to love it. She lived in that blue house on the corner, the one with the big oak tree in the front yard. That tree was struck by lightning back in '78. Split it right down the middle, sounded like a cannon going off. Woke the whole street up. The fire department had to come out because a branch fell on old Mr. Peterson's Buick. Ruined the roof completely. He was so mad he tried to sue the city, but you can't sue God for lightning, can you? That's what the judge told him anyway.

But yeah, I just feel like I've got this... this ability to get people organized, to get them to follow my lead. Like a special gift.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was saying, it's not like I can fly or read minds or anything out of a comic book. But I do get sure, I mean really sure, that I am the one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. It's like I have a special gift for making people listen and follow my plans. 

I was actually trying to explain this to the mailman the other day. He's a new fella, young kid, maybe twenty-two. Drives one of those new electric mail trucks. They're so quiet, you don't even hear them coming down the street. Not like the old ones that used to rattle and sputter. My dog, Buster—God rest his soul—used to hear the mail truck from three blocks away and start howling. Buster was a good dog, part beagle, part something else. We found him shivering under a parked car in the grocery store parking lot. The old A&P that used to be down on Main Street. They tore it down in the nineties to build a pharmacy, which is funny because now there's a pharmacy on every corner. You can't throw a rock without hitting a place selling aspirin and greeting cards. 

But anyway, yeah, I just have this gift, you know? A way of getting people to see my plans and follow along.

patient.answer:
No, no, nothing like that. I'm not a prophet or anything. I mean, I believe in the good Lord, sure, but He hasn't come down to give me any special orders or tap me on the shoulder. 

We used to go to St. Jude's every Sunday, though. Beautiful old church. They had these big stained glass windows all along the east wall. One of them got broke back in... oh, must have been '89. A bunch of kids playing baseball in the empty lot next door hit a foul ball right through the face of Saint Peter. The priest, Father Thomas, he was furious. He had this little vein in his forehead that would bulge out when he got mad. He drove a Ford Pinto, you know. Pale yellow. Worst car ever made, those Pintos. My brother-in-law Charlie bought one brand new and the heater never worked. Charlie was a pipefitter down at the plant, always had cold hands anyway. He used to carry a big metal thermos of black coffee just to keep his fingers warm on the job. Black coffee, no sugar. Said sugar was for hummingbirds. He had a glass hummingbird feeder on his back porch, used to boil the sugar water himself on the stove... 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, God's not giving me any special divine purpose or talking to me from on high. Just my own gift for getting the neighborhood together, that's all.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences delusions of grandeur or an inflated sense of self-importance, which would support a diagnosis of schizophrenia (F20.9) or a delusional disorder (F22.0).

patient.answer:
Well, I don't know about being more important, like I'm a king or a mayor or something. But I do get this feeling, this absolute certainty, that I'm the only one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. Like I've got this special gift for making folks listen and follow my plans. 

It's sort of like how my Uncle Frank used to get everyone to listen to him. He was a loud man, Frank. Worked on the railroad for forty years, laying track out west. He lost half of his left pinky finger in a coupling accident back in '52. Never stopped him from playing the accordion, though. He'd bring that heavy old thing out at Christmas and play polkas until my aunt would threaten to hide it in the attic. She kept all her old sewing patterns up in that attic. Hundreds of them, mostly from the sixties. She made me a suit once, for my cousin's wedding. It was a terrible shade of brown, like mud, but I wore it anyway because she worked so hard on it. The wedding was down at the VFW hall, the one with the leaky roof over the dance floor... 

But yeah, I just know I'm the one who can get everyone on the same page. It's my special gift.

target_item.reason: The doctor is again asking about grandiosity or feelings of unique importance and leadership abilities, which aligns with inflated self-esteem.

patient.answer:
Well, like I keep telling you, Doc, I ain't no president or nothing. But I just got this... this absolute knowing that I'm the one meant to bring the whole neighborhood together. People just naturally listen to me and want to follow the plans I make. 

You gotta have good plans, you know. You can't build a house without a blueprint. My daddy was a carpenter, built half the houses on the south side of town with his own two hands. He used one of those wooden folding rulers, kept it right in his overalls pocket. Those overalls always smelled like pine sawdust and chewing tobacco. Red Man, that was his brand. He'd spit it right into an old Folgers coffee can he kept by the porch steps. Mother hated that can. She used to grow petunias all around the porch, bright pink ones. Said the soil was good there because of the rain runoff from the gutters. We had to clean those gutters out every autumn, wet leaves piled up thick from the big oak tree out front. That tree got struck by lightning back in the summer of '65, split right down the middle like a piece of firewood... 

But, uh, yeah. I just know I'm the one to lead the neighborhood. It's my gift.

patient.answer:
Well, you know, it depends on the week. Some weeks I wake up feeling so bright and important, like I've got the sun right in my chest. I laugh loud, I talk fast, and I'm just ready to get things moving. But if folks don't listen, if they slow me down or start questioning my plans, I get real sharp with them. Real snappy. 

It reminds me of how my old dog Buster used to get. Buster was a beagle mix, had one blue eye and one brown eye. Smartest dog you ever saw, but he had no patience for the neighbor's cat. That cat was a big orange tabby, looked like a pumpkin with legs. It used to sit right on the fence post and just stare at Buster. Used to drive him crazy. Buster would bark until his voice went hoarse. We kept him on a long chain in the yard, attached to this old metal stake my daddy drove into the ground. Daddy used a sledgehammer for that. Heavy thing, probably weighed twenty pounds. He bought it at the hardware store downtown, the one Mr. Henderson used to run before he retired and moved to Florida. Florida's too hot, if you ask me. All that humidity, makes your joints ache. My cousin Martha went to Florida once for a vacation, brought back a whole bag of those little seashell soaps. Looked pretty, but they didn't lather worth a darn... 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, when I'm feeling bright and fast, I just get irritable if people don't keep up with me or question what I'm doing.

patient.answer:
Well, like I've been trying to tell you, Doc, I don't know about "great things" like being on the television or nothing. But compared to other fellas my age? Sure. I just get this absolute certainty that I'm the only one who can bring this whole neighborhood back together. I've got that special gift, you see, to make people listen and follow my plans. 

Most folks my age, they're just sitting around playing bingo down at the church basement. St. Agnes, over on 4th street. They use those little ink dabbers now, you know? Red and purple ink everywhere. Back in the day, we used those little plastic chips, the translucent red ones. You had to be real careful, because if somebody bumped the folding table, your whole card was ruined. Old man Higgins used to bump the table on purpose if he was losing. He had a terrible temper, Higgins did. Worked at the auto plant until they closed it down in '78. Drove a pale blue Ford Falcon. The muffler on that thing was completely shot, sounded like a tractor coming down the avenue. 

My brother had a tractor, a John Deere. Used it to plow his long gravel driveway in the winter. The winter of '78 was a bad one, let me tell you. Snow was piled all the way up to the porch railing. We had to melt snow on the woodstove just to have water to flush the toilet because the pipes froze solid. Took three days for the county plow to make it out to his place... 

But, anyway, I ain't just sitting around waiting to get old like the rest of them. I got my plans for the neighborhood, and I know I'm the one to do it.

patient.answer:
Well, Doc, I feel like a broken record here, but yeah, it's just like I said. I don't think I'm better than nobody in a high-and-mighty way, but I do get this absolute certainty that I'm the only one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. It's like I have a special gift, you know? A gift for making people listen and follow my plans. 

You need a good plan if you're gonna fix things up. Like when they tried to fix up the old bandstand in the park. They hired this contractor from two towns over, fella named Miller or maybe Milner. Drove a shiny new pickup truck, didn't have a speck of dirt on it. Now, you tell me, how's a man gonna do hard work if his truck is that clean? My daddy's truck was always covered in mud and drywall dust. It was a '54 Chevy, step-side. He painted it forest green himself using a brush, not a spray gun. You could see the brush strokes if you looked real close, especially on the tailgate. 

That tailgate was heavy, too. We used to sit on it and eat watermelon in the summer. The kind with the black seeds, not these seedless ones they have now. Seedless watermelon just don't taste right, if you ask me. It's like they bred all the flavor right out of it. We used to have watermelon seed spitting contests. My brother could spit a seed clear across the driveway, hit the side of the garage. The garage had this old tin roof that would rattle like crazy when the wind blew hard. Sounded like a freight train was coming right through the yard. 

But, uh, anyway... yeah. I just know I got that special gift to lead folks around here. I'm the one who can do it.

patient.answer:
Well, Doc, I feel like we're going round in circles here, like a dog chasing its own tail. But yes, I suppose you could say it sets me apart. I just get this absolute certainty, like a bell ringing clear in my head, that I'm the one who can bring the whole neighborhood together again. Like I've got this special gift for making folks listen and fall in line with my plans. 

It's a lot like how my uncle Charlie used to call the square dances down at the Grange Hall. Charlie had a voice like a foghorn, you could hear him over the fiddle and the stomping boots no problem. He'd wear these bright red suspenders and a bolo tie with a piece of turquoise the size of a robin's egg. He bought that tie out in Arizona when he went to see the Grand Canyon. Said the canyon was just a big hole in the ground, but he sure liked the jewelry. 

Charlie's wife, Aunt Bessie, she used to make the best peach cobbler for those dances. She'd use fresh peaches from the tree in their backyard, not the canned stuff. The canned stuff is always too mushy, tastes like tin. Bessie's cobbler had this thick crust on top, sprinkled with coarse sugar that would crunch when you bit into it. She baked it in this big cast-iron Dutch oven that she inherited from her grandmother. That pot must have weighed thirty pounds empty. You had to use two hands just to lift the lid. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I just have that special gift, you know? That certainty that I'm the one to lead the neighborhood.

Well, no, not really anything else. It's just like I was telling you, it's the men at the domino table, and sometimes that announcer on the radio, they're the ones giving me those little messages meant just for me. My wife, she always says it is just talk, but I know they are warning me to be careful. You gotta be careful these days. 

Especially down at the center where we play. We use the double-nine dominoes, you know. A lot of folks only use the double-six, but you need the double-nine if you've got a full table. My granddaddy had a set made of real bone. They came in this heavy wooden box with a little brass latch on the front. That latch was always sticking, though. You had to pry it open with a butter knife just to get the pieces out. We had these old butter knives with the yellow handles... bakelite, I think they called it. You don't see bakelite much anymore. Everything now is just cheap plastic. 

My wife bought a new spatula last week and the darn thing melted right in the skillet while she was frying eggs. She likes her eggs sunny-side up, but the edges have to be real crispy. You gotta use bacon grease for that, none of that vegetable oil nonsense. My regular doctor told me to watch my cholesterol, but I figure at eighty-four, I've earned a little bacon grease. 

But, uh, no... no other things sending messages. Just the radio and the domino fellas. I know they're looking out for me with those warnings, even if my wife thinks it's nothing.

patient.answer:
Well, Doc, I wouldn't say we're all part of some big grand plan or working together like that. No, it's just like I said before... I came because the men at the domino table, and sometimes that fella on the radio, they just give me these little messages. They're meant just for me, you see. My wife, she always says it's just talk, just old men flapping their gums, but I know they are warning me to be careful. 

You really do have to be careful. Like when you're crossing Elm Street down by the pharmacy. They put in that new crosswalk, but they didn't put a stoplight, just those yellow flashing lights. Nobody stops for yellow flashing lights. It's like a racetrack down there. Young kids in those little imported cars with the loud mufflers. Sounds like a swarm of angry bees coming down the road. I used to have a car that sounded like that, but it was because the exhaust pipe rusted clear through. It was a '68 Ford Fairlane. Bought it off a fella who used to race it out at the dirt track on weekends. 

He painted the whole thing primer gray. Never got around to putting a real coat of paint on it. Said primer was lighter, made the car go faster. I don't know about all that, but it sure was ugly. My wife hated that car. Refused to ride in it to church on Sundays. Said she wouldn't be caught dead arriving at the Lord's house in a primer-gray jalopy. We had to take her sister's car instead. Her sister drove this big old Buick LeSabre, the kind with the bench seats that felt like a living room sofa. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right. No, we ain't working together or nothing. It's just them warning me to be careful with those little messages. I just know what I hear, even if the wife don't believe it.

patient.answer:
Well, no, I wouldn't call it some big organized effort or some grand purpose. It's just like I've been telling you, Doc. I came in because those fellas at the domino table, and sometimes that fella on the radio, they just slip in these little messages meant just for me. My wife, she keeps saying it's just talk, just old men making noise, but I know what I hear. I know they're warning me to be careful. 

You really can't be too careful, especially with the weather turning. When the barometer drops, my left knee starts acting up. It's like a built-in weather station, better than the meteorologist on Channel 4. That fella on Channel 4, he always wears these flashy striped ties. Makes my eyes go funny just looking at him. My grandfather used to wear a tie every single day, even when he was just sitting on the front porch whittling. He’d whittle these little wooden whistles out of hickory branches. 

He had this pocket knife, a Case knife, bone handle. He kept it so sharp you could shave with it. He actually did shave with it once, just to prove he could, on a bet with my uncle. My uncle lost five dollars that day. Five dollars was a lot of money back then. You could buy a whole week's worth of groceries for five dollars. Now you can't even buy a decent cup of coffee for that. They charge you an arm and a leg for a cup of coffee, and half the time it's lukewarm. 

But anyway... what was it you asked? Oh, right. No, it's not a big organized thing. Just those little messages from the domino table and the radio, warning me to be careful, no matter what my wife thinks.

patient.answer:
Well, I wouldn't say there's a schedule, like a bus timetable or anything. It's just like I keep saying, Doc. I came because the men at the domino table, and sometimes that fella on the radio, they give me these little messages meant just for me. My wife, she always says it's just talk, but I know they are warning me to be careful. 

You gotta be careful, especially about schedules. Reminds me of when I used to take the Greyhound bus down to see my brother in Shreveport. That bus was never on schedule. You'd sit at the station for hours. The station had these hard wooden benches, the kind that make your backside numb after about ten minutes. And they always smelled like floor wax and stale cigarette smoke. Back then, everybody smoked. You could buy a pack of Chesterfields for a quarter out of a vending machine. 

Those vending machines had a heavy metal knob you had to pull, and it made this loud chunking sound. CHUNK. And the pack would drop down. Sometimes a pack of matches would come with it, tucked right under the cellophane. They don't make matches like they used to, either. Now they just bend when you try to strike them. My brother used to collect matchbooks from every place he went. Had a whole fishbowl full of them sitting on his television set. It was one of those big console TVs, the kind in the wooden cabinet that looked like a piece of furniture. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, right, a pattern. No, no real pattern to it. Just those warnings I get from the domino table and the radio, telling me to be careful, even if the wife don't see it.
